statement: A sheet of paper 0.1 mm thick is cut in half and one half is put on top of the other. The two-sheet stack is cut in half and stacked again in the same way, and so on, 20 cuts in all. Roughly how tall is the final stack?

choices.misconception: I added 0.1 mm for each of the 20 cuts instead of doubling the thickness every time.
I thought 20 doublings make 2 to the power 10 plus 2 to the power 10, about 2000 sheets, instead of 2 to the power 10 times 2 to the power 10.
I found about 100 000 mm but divided by 100 instead of by 1000 to change millimetres into metres.
I found about 100 000 mm and then read it as 100 000 m, forgetting to change the units.

hints: How many sheets are in the stack after 20 cuts?
Each cut doubles the number of sheets, so after 20 cuts there are 2 to the power 20 sheets. Estimate this using 2 to the power 10 ≈ 1000, multiply by the thickness, and change units carefully.
$2^{20} = 2^{10} \times 2^{10} \approx 1000 \times 1000$, so about a million sheets, each 0.1 mm thick.

solutions.reliable: Each cut doubles the number of sheets, so after 20 cuts there are $2^{20}$ sheets. Since $2^{10} = 1024 \approx 1000$, $2^{20}$ is about 1 000 000 (exactly 1 048 576). The height is about 1 000 000 × 0.1 mm = 100 000 mm. There are 1000 mm in a metre, so this is about 100 m (more exactly 104.9 m), the height of a tall building. The transferable idea: repeated doubling grows by a factor of about 1000 every 10 steps.

whyOnTest: Estimation questions test handling repeated doubling with the benchmark 2 to the 10th ≈ 1000, then converting units without slipping a factor of 10.
